title: States you never leave
objectives: Classify states as absorbing, transient or recurrent.
Group states into communicating classes and read cumulative absorption from $\mathbf{P}^k$

screens.title: A state with no way out
screens.prose: Here is a chain with five states. Look at the arrows that leave each one.
screens.question: Tap the state the chain can never leave once it arrives.

hints.text: Look for a state whose only arrow out is back to itself.
One state has a single loop, with chance 1.
C's only arrow is a loop labelled 1. From C, the next state is C, every time.

feedback.correct: C keeps the chain with chance 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the state whose arrows all lead back to itself.

byKey.D: D has a loop of 0.6, but its arrow of 0.4 leads to E. The chain can leave D.
byKey.E: E has a loop of 0.3, but its arrow of 0.7 leads to D. The chain can leave E.
byKey.A: A has a loop of 0.5, but half the time the chain moves to B.
byKey.B: B has no loop at all: every step the chain leaves it.

explain.text: C's only arrow is its loop with chance 1, so once the chain reaches C it stays for ever. A state with $p_{ii} = 1$ is called **absorbing**. Every other state here has an arrow that leads somewhere else.

screens.title: Where the chance goes
screens.prose: The chain starts in A, ringed. The bars show the chance of being in each state after $k$ steps, worked out exactly. Slide $k$.
screens.question: Slide to $k = 20$. Where is the chance now?

options.text: In C, D and E; A and B are almost empty
All of it in C, the absorbing state
options.why: At $k = 20$, D and E hold about 0.57 together. The chain can reach them and then never reach C.
A and B hold about 0.001 each by $k = 20$. Look at their fills.
A's loop keeps the chain only half the time each step. After 20 steps it holds about 0.001.

feedback.correct: A and B drain away into C and into the pair D, E.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the slider on 20 and read the number under each state.

explain.text: By $k = 20$ about 0.43 sits in C and 0.57 in D and E together. A and B hold almost nothing. Chance leaks out of A and B and never flows back. D and E pass it between themselves for ever.

screens.title: Coming back to A
screens.prose: Start in A again. Each step from A, the chain stays with chance 0.5 or moves to B. From B it returns to A with chance 0.3. Otherwise it goes to C or D, which never lead back.
screens.question: What is the chance the chain ever returns to A?

widget.label: Chance of ever returning to A

hints.text: Split by the first step: stay in A, or move to B.
Staying is an immediate return. Through B, the chain must take B's arrow back.
$P(\text{return}) = 0.5 + 0.5 \times 0.3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two ways back: the loop, and the trip through B.

byKey.loop-only: That counts only the loop. The chain can also go to B and come straight back.
byKey.added: You added B's 0.3 without first reaching B. That route needs $0.5 \times 0.3$.
byKey.always: The chain need not return. From B it goes to C or D with chance 0.7, and those never lead back.
byKey.via-b: That is only the route through B. The loop also returns to A, at once.

explain.text: The chain returns to A by the loop (0.5) or by the trip A, B, A ($0.5 \times 0.3 = 0.15$): 0.65 in all. So with chance 0.35 it leaves and never returns. A state you may leave and never revisit is **transient**.

screens.title: Every transient state
screens.prose: A state is **recurrent** if the chain, once there, returns to it with chance 1. Otherwise it is transient.
screens.question: Tap every transient state.

hints.text: For each state, ask: can the chain get somewhere from which it can never come back?
From D, every arrow stays inside D and E. From A or B, the chain can reach C.
A and B can lose the chain to C for good. D and E only trade the chain between themselves, so each always comes back.

feedback.correct: A and B leak; C, D and E keep the chain.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A state is transient when the chain can leave it for somewhere with no way back.

byKey.not-absorbing: You tapped every state that is not absorbing. D and E are not absorbing, but the chain always returns to each of them, so they are recurrent.
byKey.D: From D the chain goes only to E, and E sends it back. It returns to D with chance 1, so D is recurrent.
byKey.E: From E the chain goes only to D, and D sends it back. It returns to E with chance 1, so E is recurrent.
byKey.C: C is absorbing: the chain returns at every step. That makes it recurrent.
byKey.B: B is one of them. A can also lose the chain for good.
byKey.A: A is one of them. B can also lose the chain for good.

explain.text: From A or B the chain can reach C or D, and no arrow leads back from there. So A and B are transient. D and E pass the chain between themselves for ever, so each is visited again and again. C, being absorbing, is recurrent too.

screens.title: States that reach each other
screens.prose: Two states **communicate** if each can reach the other. A group of states that all communicate is a **communicating class**.
screens.question: Which set is the communicating class that contains D?

options.why: D reaches E, and E reaches D, so they belong together.
B reaches D, but D cannot reach B. Communicating needs a path each way.
C and D cannot reach each other: no arrow joins them in either direction.

hints.text: From D, which states can the chain reach? Which of those can reach D back?
D's arrows go only to D and E.
D reaches E and E reaches D. Nothing else is reachable from D.

feedback.correct: D and E form a class the chain cannot leave.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only the states with paths both ways to D.

explain.text: D and E reach each other and nothing else. So $\{D, E\}$ is a class the chain can enter but never leave: a **closed** class. The classes here are $\{A, B\}$, $\{C\}$ and $\{D, E\}$. The transient states are exactly the class that can leak out.

screens.title: Two ways to stop
screens.prose: You hold £2 and bet £1 at a time on a fair coin. You stop when you are broke or reach £4. The states are your wealth.
screens.question: What is the chance the game is over within 4 bets?

widget.accept: 0.75: after 2 bets it is over with chance 0.5; from £2 again, 2 more bets end it with chance 0.5.
widget.label: Chance the game is over within 4 bets

hints.text: Work in pairs of bets. From £2, where can you be after two bets?
After two bets you are at £0 or £4 with chance 0.25 each, or back at £2 with chance 0.5.
Over by bet 2: 0.5. Back at £2 with chance 0.5, then over by bet 4 with chance 0.5. Add $0.5 + 0.5 \times 0.5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work two bets at a time from £2.

byKey.two-bets: That is the chance it is over within 2 bets. Paths back at £2 get two more bets.
byKey.certain: A game can go £2, £3, £2, £1, £2 and still be running after 4 bets.
byKey.one-end: That is the chance of reaching one end, $\tfrac{3}{8}$. Both £0 and £4 end the game.
byKey.quarter: That is one end after 2 bets. Count both ends, and the second pair of bets.

explain.text: Two bets from £2 end the game with chance 0.5 and return you to £2 otherwise. So within 4 bets it is over with chance $0.5 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.75$. Both ends are absorbing: once there, the chain stays, so these chances only grow.

screens.title: A very sticky state
screens.prose: A lender tracks loans month by month. A loan on the Watch list stays there with chance 0.95.
screens.question: Tap every absorbing state.

hints.text: Absorbing means the loop is exactly 1, not close to 1.
Watch has two arrows out besides its loop.
Only Default has a loop of 1. Watch sends 0.03 back to Performing and 0.02 to Default each month.

feedback.correct: Only Default has a loop of exactly 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap only states whose loop is exactly 1.

byKey.sticky: You counted Watch because its loop is large. With 0.05 leaving each month, a loan leaves Watch in 20 months on average.
byKey.sticky-only: You tapped Watch for its 0.95 loop. A loan leaves it with chance 0.05 a month; only Default holds it for ever.
byKey.watch: Watch's loop is 0.95, not 1. A loan leaves it with chance 0.05 a month.
byKey.perf: Performing's loop is 0.97, not 1: 0.03 a month slips to Watch.

explain.text: A loop of 0.95 is sticky, not absorbing: each month 0.05 leaves, so a loan stays about $1/0.05 = 20$ months on average. Only Default, with a loop of exactly 1, keeps a loan for ever. And since Watch can reach Default, Watch is transient.

screens.title: No way out, and no trap either
screens.prose: A two-state regime chain: bull stays bull with chance 0.9, bear stays bear with chance 0.8.
screens.question: How should we classify the two states?

options.text: Neither is absorbing, and both are recurrent
Bull is absorbing, because 0.9 is its biggest arrow
options.why: Bull's loop is 0.9, not 1. The chain leaves it with chance 0.1 each period.

options.text: One must be absorbing: every chain has one
options.why: Many chains have none. Here the chain moves between bull and bear for ever.

options.text: Both are transient, since neither is absorbing
options.why: Transient means you might never return. From either state the chain is sure to come back.

hints.text: Is either loop exactly 1? Can the chain get stuck away from either state?
Each state sends an arrow to the other.
No loop is 1, and each state can always reach the other, so the chain keeps coming back to both.

feedback.correct: One class, closed, with both states recurrent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the loops, then ask whether the chain can escape for good from either state.

explain.text: Neither loop is 1, so neither state is absorbing. Bull and bear reach each other and nothing else, so they form one closed class. The chain returns to each with chance 1. Not every chain has an absorbing state, and this one is all recurrent.

screens.title: The three kinds of state
screens.prose: Write $f_i$ for the chance that a chain starting in $i$ ever returns to $i$. You found $f_A = 0.65$. $$\text{absorbing: } p_{ii} = 1, \qquad \text{transient: } f_i < 1, \qquad \text{recurrent: } f_i = 1.$$ An absorbing state is recurrent, with $f_i = 1$ at once.
screens.question: In a chain with finitely many states, state $i$ can reach some state $j$ that cannot reach $i$. What is $i$?

options.why: If the chain goes to $j$, it can never return. That happens with positive chance, so $f_i < 1$.
An absorbing state reaches only itself. This one reaches $j$.
Any positive chance of reaching $j$ is enough: from there the return is impossible.

feedback.correct: A way out with no way back makes $f_i < 1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what happens to the chance of returning once the chain reaches $j$.

explain.text: With some chance the chain reaches $j$, and from $j$ it can never get back to $i$. So $f_i < 1$ and $i$ is transient, as A and B were. In a finite chain the converse holds too: a state with no such escape is recurrent.

screens.title: Default by year k
screens.prose: Back to the bank's ratings, A, B and Default, with default absorbing. The bars show $(\mathbf{P}^k)_{AD}$ for a loan rated A today, which you met for $k = 3$.
screens.question: What is the chance the loan defaults during year 3, not before?

hints.text: Default is absorbing. What does $(\mathbf{P}^3)_{AD}$ count?
Being in D at year 3 means defaulting in year 1, 2 or 3.
Take the loans in D by year 2 away from those in D by year 3: $0.0519 - 0.028$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each bar counts every loan in default by then. Subtract to isolate one year.

byKey.cumulative: That is the chance of being in default by year 3. Because D is absorbing, it already includes the loans that defaulted in years 1 and 2.
byKey.one-step: That is the first year's chance from A. By year 3 some loans have slipped to B, where default is likelier.
byKey.year2: That is the default in year 2: $0.028 - 0.01$. Move one bar along.
byKey.summed: You added the bars. Each bar already contains the ones before it, so subtract instead.

explain.text: Because Default is absorbing, $(\mathbf{P}^k)_{AD}$ is the chance of having defaulted by year $k$: the bars only rise. A default during year 3 is in the third bar but not the second: $0.0519 - 0.0280 = 0.0239$. The yearly rate climbs, from 0.010 to 0.018 to 0.024, as loans drift to B.

ideas: An absorbing state has $p_{ii} = 1$: once there, the chain stays. A loop of 0.95 is sticky, not absorbing.
A transient state can be left for good ($f_i < 1$); a recurrent one is always revisited ($f_i = 1$). In a finite chain, a state is transient when it can reach a state that cannot reach it back.
States that reach each other form a communicating class. Not every chain has an absorbing state: the bull and bear chain is one closed, recurrent class.

formula.name: Return probability
formula.tex: f_i = P(\text{the chain returns to } i \mid X_0 = i), \quad \text{transient: } f_i < 1, \quad \text{recurrent: } f_i = 1
formula.note: Absorbing means $p_{ii} = 1$, so $f_i = 1$ at the first step.

summary.trap: A large loop is not a loop of 1. And a state that is not absorbing need not be transient: D and E were recurrent.

quiz.prose: An order is New, Partially filled, Filled or Cancelled. Filled and Cancelled orders never change again; New and Partial orders can still fill or be cancelled.
quiz.question: Which states are absorbing? Select all that apply.

options.why: A new order can fill, partly fill or be cancelled, so it can leave New.
A partly filled order can still fill or be cancelled.

feedback.correct: Filled and Cancelled each have a loop of 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Absorbing states are the ones the order never leaves.

explain.text: Filled and Cancelled are terminal: their loops are 1, so both are absorbing, and every order ends in one of them. New and Partial are transient.

quiz.prose: State $i$ has a loop of 0.7. Its only other arrow, 0.3, leads to an absorbing state.
quiz.question: What is $f_i$, the chance of ever returning to $i$?

widget.accept: 0.7: the loop is the only way back.
widget.label: Chance of returning

feedback.correct: Only the loop returns, so $f_i = 0.7$: transient.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the ways back to $i$.

byKey.one: With chance 0.3 the first step leads into the absorbing state, and the chain never returns.
byKey.three: That is the chance of leaving for good. You want the chance of returning.

explain.text: The first step either loops back (0.7) or enters the absorbing state, from which there is no return (0.3). So $f_i = 0.7 < 1$ and $i$ is transient.

quiz.prose: A colleague says every Markov chain eventually gets stuck in an absorbing state.
quiz.question: Which chain shows the claim is false?

options.text: Bull and bear, with loops 0.9 and 0.8
Gambler's ruin from £2, stopping at £0 or £4
options.why: That chain has two absorbing states and does get stuck in one of them.
Default has a loop of 1, so that chain does have an absorbing state.

options.text: An order's life, ending Filled or Cancelled
options.why: Filled and Cancelled are absorbing, so the claim holds there.

feedback.correct: The regime chain has no absorbing state.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a chain where no loop equals 1.

explain.text: In the regime chain neither loop is 1, and the chain switches between bull and bear for ever. Both states are recurrent and none is absorbing, so the claim fails.

quiz.prose: For the bank's A loan, $(\mathbf{P}^4)_{AD} = 0.0800$ and $(\mathbf{P}^5)_{AD} = 0.1111$. Default is absorbing.
quiz.question: What is the chance the loan defaults during year 5?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the chance of default by year 4.

byKey.cumulative: That is default by year 5, including earlier years. Subtract the year-4 figure.
byKey.summed: You added. Each figure already includes the earlier years, so subtract.

explain.text: Because Default is absorbing, $(\mathbf{P}^k)_{AD}$ counts every default up to year $k$. The ones in year 5 alone are $0.1111 - 0.0800 = 0.0311$.
